content:
I noticed recently that Apple appears to have given up on Cinematic Mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my disappointment.

The issue isn't that this feature is bad, but rather that it's so close to being truly useful that it makes it even harder to understand why Apple hasn't taken advantage of the massive performance gains between the iPhone 13 that first introduced this feature and the latest iPhones. Let me show you…

I've previously explained why I understand Apple not prioritising updates to this feature, but I also believe Apple should update it so that it can encourage future video creators and filmmakers—especially young people who may not have other camera equipment.

I have a friend who likes to use his smartphone to approach random strangers on the street and ask them to say something unexpected. I decided to flip the situation and asked him to sit on a bench, then filmed him with a smartphone—my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to test how complex a scene Cinematic Mode could handle: a person sitting in the foreground, a railing about 25 feet behind him, a river beyond that, and the O2 Arena roughly a thousand feet further back. And because he was sitting on a bench, his range of movement was quite limited.

The answer is…very close, but not quite there. The overall effect is decent, but there are noticeable haloing issues around his legs and the railing, and when his movement crosses the support structures of the O2 Arena, those structures sometimes come into focus. When he stretches out his hands, the river behind him occasionally snaps into focus:

To be fair, CK thought that most people watching the footage probably wouldn't notice the issue. If they're not filmmakers or tech enthusiasts familiar with how this feature works, they likely won't see these flaws at all—or if they do, they won't find them distracting. I think he might be right.

But this is what truly frustrates me: I believe even amateur film enthusiasts would share my disappointment—and these are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the beginning, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I genuinely believe that if Apple properly leveraged the computational power and neural network capabilities of current iPhone chips, this feature could be dramatically improved. In fact, I'd expect a properly updated Cinematic Mode to handle scenes far more complex than this one.

Do you agree with my view? Do you want Apple to take Cinematic Mode seriously? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
